newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-LONRHO CHIEF SELLS STAKE TO ANGLO .
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-LONRHO CHIEF SELLS STAKE TO ANGLO .

text.p: German financier Dieter Bock, the man who deposed Tiny Rowland as head of the Lonrho conglomerate after a fierce boardroom battle, on Tuesday sold all his shares in the company and said he would step down as chief executive.
The moves were part of Bock's plan to head up the trading business of Lonrho once it has been carved up into three separate firms, Lonrho said in a statement.
Bock sold his 18.3 percent stake in Lonrho to South African mining giant Anglo American .
The lawyer-turned-property magnate joined Lonrho in February 1993, but the relationship between him and the controversial Rowland quickly turned sour.
Their often public rows culminated in March 1995 when Rowland was ousted from the Lonrho board 34 years after the still sprightly tycoon, who is now 78 years old, founded the company.
Lonrho said Bock's decision to step down as chief executive and become a non-executive deputy chairman would give the company freedom in completing its planned break-up.
The firm's three-way split into separate mining, hotels and trading firms was devised by Bock shortly after he had toppled business tycoon Rowland.
Bock has said he wants to take a financial stake in the trading arm, which involves car dealerships and agricultural commodities, primarily centred in Africa.
The trading division will be spun off once the hotels are sold. An announcement on the sale of the hotels is expected shortly.
Speculation about possible buyers of the two chains -- Metropole and Princess -- has focused respectively on British hotel operator Stakis and Saudi billionaire investor Prince al-Waleed bin Talal.

Once the hotels and the trading arms have been divested, Lonrho will be left with its mining operations which include a 30 percent stake in Ghana's ashanti Goldfields , one of the world's biggest gold mining companies.
Anglo American is particularly interested in the Ashanti stake, but has said in the past it will not make a full offer for Lonrho.
Lonrho said Bock is stepping out of the limelight to avoid suspicions that he is completing the demerger process on terms best suited to his own interests.

"He doesn't want to be in a position of influence at a time when decisions on how to demerge are being made because he has already said he wants to become an investor in the trading operation," a Lonrho spokesman said.
Lonrho said the imminent sale of the hotels would enable Bock to step down and be succeeded as chief executive by deputy managing director Nick Morrell.
Lonrho welcomed the fact that Anglo American had tightened its links with the group, increasing its stake to 25.9 percent.
"(This)...will further strengthen our ability to develop our mining interests," Bock said in a statement.
The stake sale to Anglo follows an agreement reached in April under which Bock acquired the right to sell his stake at 180 pence.
Lonrho's share rose 4 1/2 pence to close at 163 1/2 p following the news.
